sm: The Williamson County Board of Commissioners opens its November 9th, 2026 meeting with an invocation by Commissioner Jefferson and the Pledge of Allegiance, followed by a roll call with all commissioners present. The chairman welcomes Commissioner Sturgeon back in person. Three late-filed resolutions, numbered 1126-28, 1126-29 and 1126-30, are accepted onto the agenda without objection. The minutes of the October 12th meeting are approved on a motion by Commissioner Mitchell, seconded by Commissioner Cardin. In citizens communications, Cecilia Shevlin of Spring Hill warns about AI data centers, quoting a Texas landowner who called hyperscale centers unnecessary, and notes that Murray County has a twelve-month moratorium running until June 2027.

Cecilia Shevlin finishes by noting sixteen data centers are planned in Tennessee this year, with sixty-one already operating, and urges the commission to consider a moratorium of twelve months or more on hyper and medium scale compute campuses. Mayor Andy Marshall then presents recognitions. November is proclaimed Family Court Awareness Month, accepted by a representative of the Barron Foundation. He also notes that Chris and Elaine Whitney, founders of One Gen Away, celebrated fifty million meals served, with a goal of five hundred million. Finally, he reads a proclamation honoring the Franklin High School girls volleyball team, which won the state Class AAA championship on October 23rd, finishing thirty-three and one without dropping a set in the tournament.

The mayor reads a proclamation honoring first responders who rescued bicyclist Jason Tatum, who fell about 200 feet down a cliff off Old Highway 96 on August 15th, 2026. A sheriff's deputy found his bicycle, and crews from multiple agencies carried out a high angle rope rescue before he was airlifted to Vanderbilt. Mr. Tatum has since recovered. Commissioners Jones and Mitchell brought this forward. Next, representatives of the Employer Support of the Guard and Reserve, including retired Colonel Eric Rosoloski, begin a presentation recognizing Sheriff Jeff Hughes and the Sheriff's Department for supporting employees who serve in the Guard and Reserve.

Lieutenant Hickman, a reservist, praises Sheriff Hughes for supporting guardsmen and reservists, mentioning a luncheon for veterans and care packages for deployed staff. Sheriff Hughes receives the Seven Seals Award, after the department earlier received another award at a summer conference. In the county mayor's report, Jeff Drummond is introduced as the nominee for the first appointment to the NES board, and ten employees were honored for thirty years of service. Finance reports September education impact fee collections of 1.7 million dollars, down about 453,000 from August, and privilege tax collections of about 1.2 million. The Cool Springs Conference Center earned a net operating profit of 92,107 dollars for the month, bringing the fiscal year total to 116,924 dollars.

Schools Director Dr. Lee Webb praises the Franklin High volleyball team and notes that several Williamson County elementary and middle schools were named tops in the state by US News and World Report. He describes the district's first quarter review of data on transportation, maintenance response and classrooms, and collaboration with similar districts such as one in Olathe, Kansas. The district received a 10.8 million dollar federal geothermal tax rebate for Arrington, Amanda North and Page High, which must be spent on capital projects and will come to the commission in January. The district expects about 5 million more for Brentwood Middle. Mayor Marshall says a public information manager offer was made that morning, with two finalists interviewed. The Williamson Health report then begins.

The Williamson Health chief thanks the foundation for recent events, including honors awards on September 19th and a golf classic on October 5th, and lists recognitions such as a coronary imaging quality award, two US News best hospital awards for back surgery and hip replacement, and a top ten percent ranking for heart attack treatment. Williamson Parent Magazine named it best hospital and best place to have a baby. November is Lung Cancer Awareness Month. The financial report shows September operating income of about 2.97 million dollars, or 8.6 percent of net revenue, against a budget of 2.6 million. Year to date net income is 364,000 dollars against a budget of 66,000. Days cash on hand is 111, up four days from the prior month. Parks and Recreation is then invited to report.

Gordon Hampton, in his first report as Parks and Recreation director, gives numbers. The county has a 903 million dollar budget, and Parks and Recreation's portion is slightly over 24 million. The department returned 1.8 million in unused funds and generated about 13.2 million in revenue, leaving its actual cost at about 9.3 million, or 1.03 percent of the county budget. Over 260,000 accounts have registered for programs in the past decade, with about 40,918 active this year. The Performing Arts Center sold 25,777 tickets and the Renaissance Festival sold 93,213. Roughly 160,000 unique participants were counted in a county of about 250,000. Recreation centers saw nearly 600,000 visits, there were 31,109 athletic users, and nature parks drew about 176,000 visitors.

Hampton says the Ag Expo Park completed its first full operating cycle, with 213 bookings, 59 major events drawing 488,700 attendees, and 154 meeting room events, totaling close to 500,000 people. He plans feasibility studies and requests for proposals, and says the building has had no major capital work in over twenty-five years. Commissioner Floyd asks about water issues on Bethesda Road, and Hampton says a timeline is being prepared and he meets with the contractor Thursday. Commissioners Sturgeon and Petty ask about nonresident users and Ag Expo income. Then elections begin. Lee Jorgensen is nominated to the emergency communications board for districts one and two, and the vote proceeds. For districts eight and nine, Mac Purdy is nominated, and Commissioner Beasley notes the packet lacked biographies.

The Purdy appointment passes after staff apologize that biographies were omitted from the packet. Jeff Drummond is nominated to the electric power board for a term running January 2027 to July 2029, Patty Hinton to the Planning Commission, and Saul Hirschbein as judicial commissioner for a one-year term, each moving to a vote. The consent agenda is approved, with Commissioner Tonnakloff abstaining due to employment and Commissioner Todd abstaining as a notary. Resolution 10-26-24, a tower lease agreement with Vogue Tower Partner Seven LLC, passes twenty-four to zero. The commission then opens a public hearing on resolution 11-26-4, creating the Arrington Village zoning district. Emily Bowman, whose family farm dates to the late 1800s, raises concerns about traffic and farm access.

Emily Bowman asks that the vote be deferred, urging the commission to weigh the proposed boundaries against the comprehensive plan's commitment to family farms and rural preservation, including protections for traffic, drainage and a clear transition to rural land. Kim Hill, whose family has lived on Wilson Pike since 1964, describes flooding of the creek near her father's property and asks the commission to deny or at least defer. Jane Perro of Trinity Road wants to keep Arrington as a hamlet and update its rules, questioning whether the 39 parcel owners were asked to join, noting that sign-ins at public meetings fell from 146 to 34, and saying the yellow zoning signs had blown away.

Jane Perro asks whether commissioners have been briefed, citing the loss of rural character in Triune, and asks for deferral. John Hoover of Lake Colonial Estates, an Arrington fire board secretary, says the district grows by 75 to 100 acres originally zoned for one house per five acres, which at two houses per acre could mean 150 to 200 houses. Another speaker, from Burke Hollow Road, calculates that of 325 study acres about 90 are floodplain, and the draft could allow 470 houses in a traditional layout or about 280 in a conservation layout. He favors one unit per acre, saying Arrington lacks the commercial activity of other special area plan sites.

The Burke Hollow Road speaker finishes by saying he is fine with either path as long as Arrington stays rural. Julie Warpool, a member of the advisory committee and a farm family resident, supports the village designation, saying residents wanted coffee shops and small businesses, and that current hamlet rules would allow a liquor store and three-story buildings. Will Parker says many residents learned of the plan only from signs or community news, and asks how boundaries were set and how many owners were asked, requesting deferral. Linda Artemov of Nolensville asks for deferral and worries about traffic on Highway 96. Kelly Paris of Patton Road questions whether the 2020 Williamson 2040 assumptions still hold.

Kelly Paris asks whether hamlet regulations could be updated with protections instead of redesignating, and urges the commission to preserve rural character. Public comment closes. Commissioner Goodspeed moves, seconded by Commissioner Torres, to adopt resolution 11-26-4. A planning commissioner explains that a task force developed the resolution and that revisions made at the planning meeting are included. Commissioner Floyd says most speakers opposed it, questions the one to two percent attendance at meetings, and moves to defer for more public engagement, seconded by Commissioner Sturgeon. Rules require a specific date, and February 8th is proposed. Planning staff ask for direction on what to do in the interim, noting the Planning Commission must also approve any changes.

Commissioner Floyd says he has no specific date in mind but wants enough time for citizens to be heard. Commissioner Lawrence asks about notification, and planning staff say letters went to property owners before the process began about two years ago, and to affected and adjacent owners for each hearing, plus signs, newspaper notice, social media and flyers. Lawrence suggests another public meeting at the school. Staff explain that any change to what is presented must return to the Planning Commission, with thirty days of newspaper notice for each hearing, so the holidays make a February 8th return tight.

Staff say February 8th might have to be pushed back if changes are made, because each public hearing requires thirty days of notice. Commissioner Williams asks about the origin of the proposal, the pros and cons of hamlet versus village, and whether deferral is the right action. Planning staff say the 2020 comprehensive plan recommended converting Arrington Hamlet to a village after a special area plan. The hamlet has allowed nonresidential uses since 1988, and the new standards add design criteria. The study area grew by 75 to 100 acres, much of it floodplain. Commissioner Fellhauer favors sending density back to planning. Commissioner Todd asks how the added land came in, how staying a hamlet would affect growth, and how a village would protect farmland.

Staff explain the hamlet grew about 20 to 30 percent because many properties from the late 1980s were split-zoned, and Roberts Road offered a logical boundary with shallow, flood-prone lots. They say the hamlet or village designation does not really influence whether farms continue, and the village standards remove objectionable uses and improve design. They agree to look at the added acreage and density if the commission wishes. Commissioner Sturgeon supports revising the plan, removing dense development, and giving the public one more chance. The motion is amended to defer to the March meeting, which is on March 8th, 2027, and Sturgeon agrees.

Commissioner Varell questions planning staff. Density in the hamlet is two units per acre for traditional subdivisions, and the village keeps it at two. Staff estimate the added acreage would yield less than half the theoretical maximum because of lot sizes, roads, floodplain and buffers. A bar or tavern is currently allowed, with green space required for nonresidential uses, and a craft distillery would need ninety percent green space. Staff say they could not require mixed uses under current language. There is no data center use defined in the ordinance, so an applicant's letter of intent would be compared with similar uses. If deferred, a developer could still propose a project meeting current standards, which must be evaluated under existing zoning.

Staff say that if the zoning passed now and the commission later wanted changes such as lowering density to one and a half units per acre, it would take the Planning Commission in December or January and return to the commission in February or March. Commissioner Tonnakloff asks for napkin math on additional houses, noting only one speaker supported the plan. Commissioner Goodspeed praises the planning work and asks whether deferral can pause development proposals, and staff say they cannot hold a determined applicant. Staff say the district could be renamed Arrington Hamlet. Commissioner Petty notes about ninety percent of the yard signs were down and supports one more chance for public input, noting the last meeting drew about 63 people.

Commissioner Sturgeon asks how family subdivisions were added to the village standards, and staff say it was done with the advisory committee because people generally want them. Staff agree to revisit the density of 1.2 units per acre for conservation subdivisions and two for traditional ones. Commissioners thank the planning team and express support for one more meeting. The motion to defer resolution 11-26-4 to March 8th, 2027, passes twenty-three to zero, with Commissioner Sanford excused, and another public hearing will be held then. After a five minute break, the board takes up resolution 11-26-5, an intent to fund 87 million dollars for a new middle school on Split Log Road. Commissioner Williams offers an amendment saying the money comes from education impact fees and striking language about tax-exempt bond reimbursement.

The amendment passes twenty-three to zero with one absent. Commissioner Mason asks Dr. Webb about future needs, since the education impact fee fund holds about 100 million dollars. Dr. Webb says Midland Middle is at capacity, Mill Creek is nearly full, and Sunset is close, with about 18 developments and 3,000 homes underway in the area, and the sites cannot be expanded. Finance director Phoebe says impact fees average about 20 million dollars a year, so the fund should still hold about 30 million at year end. The January appropriation could fund about 45 million first, with the rest later. Commissioner Herbrey, concerned that enrollment is falling and some schools are half full, begins to ask for a deferral.

Commissioner Herbrey moves to defer to January so the school board can study rezoning and additions, but the motion dies for lack of a second. Dr. Webb tells Commissioner Goodspeed that the first draw would cover design and bidding, noting rock on the site, that district bus routes aim for no more than one hour, and that portables are possible as a stopgap. Initial staffing for a new building costs about 2.5 million dollars. Commissioner Williams says enrollment has plateaued and the demographics are older, warns of a tough budget year, and says the school board must consider rezoning. He says closing under-capacity schools may need discussion, and the commission is not simply approving prior plans.

Dr. Webb tells Commissioner Sturgeon that the district is evaluating how to repurpose emptying buildings, whether through revenue, innovation or sale, and will recommend to the board in the next few months and keep the commission informed. Commissioner Petty asks about portable security, and Webb says each addition gets a safety assessment. The rock on site is included in the 87 million dollar figure. Commissioner Todd asks whether any impact fee funds face a spending deadline, citing six to ten years. Finance says collections have been tracked in five-year increments since 2017 and debt payments were placed strategically to stay on track, though she had no exact figure at hand.

Finance says the funds are restricted to bonds tied to prior education impact funds, and that this use was planned with the school district. Dr. Webb tells Commissioner Beasley the school board voted unanimously for the intent to fund, with rezoning recommendations expected this fall. Woodland Middle is at 100 percent, Mill Creek at 96 and Sunset near 90. The intent to fund passes twenty-three to one. Resolution 11-26-6 would move 100,000 dollars for a superintendent search because of the vacancy of Superintendent Golden. A commissioner objects that searches go poorly and that home-grown Dr. Webb is the best choice, and says he will vote no.

Resolution 11-26-6 passes seventeen to seven. The commission then approves, each twenty-four to zero, a capital budget amendment of 1,577,665 dollars for e-rate reimbursement, a 4,480 dollar state library grant, a 20,330 dollar state museum grant, and a library budget increase of 19,248 dollars from donations and fees. It also approves 66,220 dollars in rollover opioid abatement funds for the DUI recovery court, and a resolution distributing the county's opioid settlement funds to proposals chosen by the task force. A Parks and Recreation donation appropriation of 138,955 dollars and 92 cents is on the floor, and the vote is recorded in the next part.

The Parks and Recreation donations resolution passes twenty-four to zero. A 32,000 dollar state highway safety grant for the Sheriff's Office passes, and Commissioner Floyd later says he abstains on sheriff items because he works there. Resolution 11-26-15 appropriates 1,205,000 dollars to the self-insurance fund from fund balance. Commissioner Mason notes it was not unanticipated, since an extra 1,000 dollars per employee was removed at budget time. Finance says claims were 2.3 million dollars in one week and 21.8 million in three months, against about 120 million last year, and a school-side resolution of about 5 million will come in January. It passes twenty-four to zero. A 189,000 dollar Sheriff's equitable share appropriation is introduced.

The Sheriff's equitable share appropriation passes twenty-four to zero. Late-filed resolution 11-26-28 raises the per diem for unsalaried public records commission members from 25 to 100 dollars, and passes. Late-filed 11-26-30 accepts a four million dollar state grant for the Limestone Creek wastewater provider in Grassland, and also passes. Resolution 11-26-16 renews the mattress recycling agreement, amended on Commissioner Mason's motion to delete the word pilot, and passes twenty-four to zero. Resolution 11-26-17 overrides the City of Franklin's denial regarding roof mechanical equipment visibility at the proposed juvenile justice center, which is on county-owned adjacent land, and its vote begins.

The juvenile justice center override passes twenty-four to zero. The commission then approves, each twenty-four to zero, a contract to buy property at 3727 New Highway 96 West for a west county fire station and ambulance facility, and a long-term lease with the school district for property at 300 Beasley Drive. It also approves declaring Sheriff's Office motorcycles surplus, as the office replaces Harley-Davidsons with three BMW motorcycles, and declaring law enforcement equipment surplus. Two furniture donations pass, and so does a donation of five air packs from Williamson County Fire Rescue. Resolution 11-26-25, an interlocal agreement for emergency ambulance services with Williamson Health, Spring Hill and Murray County, is introduced with questions from Commissioner Mason.

Commissioner Mason explains that Spring Hill straddles two counties and that Williamson County has covered the Murray County side for six years. She says Murray County's budget committee that night asked for a six-month extension instead of signing. Staff say Williamson Health has covered the costs from July 1st to January 1st, and that the proposed eighteen-month agreement, with 750,000 dollars for six months and 1.5 million dollars for the following year, was a handshake deal with the Murray County mayor in September. They say it gives time to stabilize staffing. Commissioner Tonnecliff notes Spring Hill leaders want eighteen months. Commissioner Varell learns Murray's budget committee voted only to appropriate for six months.

A commissioner asks what happens if Murray County approves only six months. Legal counsel says the contract as written would require Murray to fund next year, and material changes would return to the commission, which does not meet in December unless a special meeting is called. The commissioner says he is disappointed Williamson taxpayers are covering Murray County but supports the offer. The ambulance agreement is voted on. The last item, resolution 11-26-26, adopts the commission's rules, with an amendment to attach the rules committee's revised version, which passes twenty-four to zero. The main motion as amended also passes twenty-four to zero. Members are reminded of a Veterans Day reception at the county archives and the parade in downtown Franklin, and the meeting adjourns.
